1. The animation shows how much total interest a mortgage costs under two plans. A 30-year loan on its normal schedule costs $477,622 in interest. The same 30-year loan, if paid off in 15 years, costs $210,691. The labels "Freddie Mac weekly mortgage survey" and "ILLUSTRATIVE" mark the figures as example numbers based on US rate history. "US only · history, not a forecast" is also on screen.

2. A stack of green cash piles grows. In frame 1 a small stack sits beside two gray bars with gold tops, which look like the loan balance or principal. By frames 2 and 3 the stack is very tall and labeled with the 30-year interest of $477,622. In frames 4 to 6 the stack is shifted into place beside the gray bars. A second, much shorter stack then appears, labeled "30-year paid in 15: $210,691."

3. Paying a mortgage off faster cuts the total interest a lot. In this example, paying the 30-year loan off in 15 years saves roughly $267,000 in interest, which is more than half of what the 30-year schedule would cost.

4. A viewer would probably take away that paying a loan off early saves a large amount of interest. The animation does not say whether to prepay or invest instead. It doesn't show investment returns, risk, or the viewer's own rate or finances. It also gives no recommendation for your $320,000 loan.

5. The picture and on-screen text show the interest comparison only. The idea that paying early saves money is a natural reading of the two stacks. Any advice to prepay, or to invest instead, would be my own conclusion and not something the animation says.
